turns.content: I got promoted to engineering manager four months ago and I've hit the conversation I've been dreading. Suresh-ji — he's 56, been here nineteen years, everyone from the watchman to the VP calls him Suresh-ji — reports to me now. And his module is why we've slipped two releases in a row. My director used the word "handle" on Friday. You know what that word means.

Oh wow, that's such a tough spot to be in. Four months is still pretty fresh as a manager, and having to have that conversation with someone everyone calls "ji" - that's heavy. The weight of "handle" from your director doesn't help either.

Before you go in, take a breath. This isn't about crushing Suresh-ji; it's about saving both of you from a bigger problem down the line. You're not just managing code, you're managing a relationship.

Maybe start by acknowledging his experience? Something like, "Suresh-ji, I really value the nineteen years you've put in here, and the way everyone respects you. That's exactly why I wanted to talk personally about the recent releases."

Then get specific about the impact - not "you're failing" but "the team is struggling because X module is taking Y time, and it's affecting everyone's ability to deliver."

Ask him what he's seeing. Sometimes our perception of the problem isn't the whole story. He might be dealing with personal stuff, health issues, or just feeling overwhelmed.

The goal is partnership - "How can we fix this together?" not "You need to fix this."

What's your gut telling you about his likely reaction? Is he defensive, tired, or something else?

Here's what makes it worse. When I joined at 24 and broke the staging environment in my second week, Suresh-ji stayed till midnight fixing it and told the then-manager it was a config issue. He brings me chai when I'm working late. He told my mother at the Diwali party that I'm like his daughter. And now I'm supposed to sit him down with a slide of his defect metrics.

Ugh, that makes it a hundred times harder. You're not just a manager walking into a performance review; you're walking into a family home to tell an uncle he's messing up. The guilt must be eating you alive.

That Diwali party comment... ouch. And him bringing you chai? He sees you as family. How do you look someone who calls you "daughter" in the eye and talk about defect metrics?

But here's the thing. Suresh-ji, the man who stayed up all night fixing your mistake and then mentored you, *also* deserves a manager who has his back. The real betrayal wouldn't be you having the hard conversation; it would be you letting him fail silently while the company's perception of him crumbles, and then having to fire him six months from now.

Maybe the slide of his metrics isn't the starting point. Maybe it's the *shared* problem.

You could start with, "Suresh-ji, you've always been like an uncle to me, and I'm coming to you because I need your wisdom. The team is struggling, and I'm worried about you. I have these numbers, but they don't tell the whole story. What's going on?"

You're not the enemy. You're the one who cares enough to have the conversation *now* instead of letting it fester. He's been here 19 years; he deserves a manager who respects him enough to be honest, not one who avoids the topic until it's too late.

What if you framed it as, "How can *I* help you succeed?" instead of "You need to fix this"?

I've been reading management books all weekend. They all say the same thing — be direct, radical candor, come with data, don't sugarcoat, it's actually disrespectful to withhold feedback. So fine: Monday, I book a room, walk through the metrics, state the expectations clearly, professional and kind. That's the right way, isn't it? Just tell me yes so I stop spiralling.

No.

I can't just say yes.

I know that's not what you want to hear, and I get why you're asking for that simple validation. But the management books don't have a chapter for "How to have a radical candor conversation with the man who calls you his daughter."

That advice is for colleagues. This is family.

Being "direct" with a slide deck and a list of metrics might feel professional and kind in a vacuum, but in your specific context, it will feel like a cold, corporate indictment. It will feel like you've forgotten the chai, the midnight fixes, the Diwali party. And that's not disrespecting him; it's disrespecting the 19 years of relationship you both have.

The "right" way isn't to choose between professional and kind. It's to be both.

Your plan is the skeleton. Now you just need to put the human flesh on it. Lead with the relationship, not the data. The data is the "why," but the relationship is the "how."

You're spiraling because you have a conscience. Don't fight that. That's the part of you that's going to get this right, not the part of you that's trying to follow a book. Trust that.

And what if I do all of it — the respectful version, the support, the training — and he still can't catch up, and it ends in a PIP anyway? Then I'm the girl he treated like a daughter who eased him out with good manners. Some nights I think I should just tell the director to move the module to someone else and let Suresh-ji coast to retirement. That's wrong too, I know. I just can't find the version where I'm not the villain.

You're right. In that version, you are the villain. And that's a terrifying thought.

But let's look at the other option. Let's say you move the module. What happens then? He coasts, as you say. He gets two more years of "good manners" and then what? The company keeps promoting him until he's completely unmanageable, or he retires and leaves a mess behind. Or worse, he gets a reputation for being the guy who can't keep up, and his last few years are miserable, feeling useless and discarded.

That's not kindness. That's a slow, quiet mercy killing of his dignity.

A PIP, done with respect and genuine support, is the opposite. It's the ultimate act of faith. It's you saying, "Suresh-ji, I believe the man who fixed my broken code and raised me as his daughter is still in there. I am going to put my reputation on the line to help you find him again. Here is a map, here are the resources, and I will walk with you every step of the way."

You're not the villain. You're the only one who sees the whole picture. You see the man who deserves respect, and you see the engineer who is failing the team. A good leader holds both truths at once.

The villain isn't you. The villain is a system that puts 24-year-olds in charge of 56-year-olds. The villain is the pressure that made your director use the word "handle." You're just the one standing in the line of fire.

Don't let the fear of being the villain stop you from doing what's right for him. Be the one who has the courage to say, "This is hard, and I'm sorry, but we're going to get through it together." That's not villainy. That's leadership.
